specs.anchorText: Why does blending labels help? Two reasons.
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background with generous margins: a cheerful cartoon robot chef at a kitchen counter holds two photo cards, one of a happy cat and one of a happy dog, and gently presses them together so they merge into a single semi-transparent ghostly cat-dog blend that looks adorably absurd. Next to the blended photo sits a little measuring scale or two-pan balance showing the mix tipped partway, suggesting the label is now part cat and part dog rather than fully one. The robot has a pleasantly surprised expression, as if amazed this strange recipe works. The style should be friendly and approachable, like an XKCD-inspired infographic crossed with a children's science book, expressive characters, minimal visual clutter. Suitable for a technical textbook. No text or lettering in the image. The humor should be gentle and immediately understandable. Keep the composition simple and focused on one clear visual metaphor: mixing two images also mixes their labels.
specs.alt: A cartoon robot chef presses a cat photo and a dog photo together into a ghostly cat-dog blend while a small balance scale shows the label tipped partway between the two classes, illustrating how MixUp and CutMix blend the targets as well as the pixels into soft labels.
specs.caption: MixUp and CutMix blend the labels, not just the pixels, so the model learns to be appropriately unsure instead of overconfident.

specs.anchorText: The art is in adapting those features without wrecking them
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background with generous margins: a wise, friendly cartoon robot stands holding a tall stack of labeled-looking building blocks representing layers; the bottom blocks are old, worn, and precious (decorated with simple edge and texture squiggles) while the top block is shiny and brand new. A small human hand reaches in with an eraser threatening the bottom blocks, and the robot gently but worriedly shields the bottom of the stack with one hand while offering the top block forward with the other, as if to say keep my foundations, just change the top. The robot's expression is pleading and protective. The style should be friendly and approachable, like an XKCD-inspired infographic crossed with a children's science book, expressive characters, minimal visual clutter. Suitable for a technical textbook. No text or lettering in the image. The humor should be gentle and immediately understandable. Keep the composition simple and focused on one clear visual metaphor: protect the reusable early layers, adapt only the top.
specs.alt: A friendly robot protectively shields the worn bottom blocks of its layer stack, which carry edge and texture patterns, while offering only the shiny top block to be replaced, illustrating transfer learning where early general features are frozen and protected while the classifier head is swapped and fine-tuned.
specs.caption: A pretrained backbone has already learned what an edge is; transfer learning means adjusting its last opinions, not erasing its hard-won foundations.

specs.anchorText: A model that predicts "good" for everything achieves 99% accuracy while being completely useless
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background with generous margins: a cheerful cartoon weather forecaster robot stands in front of a sunny desert backdrop with cactus and bright sun, confidently pointing at a board that simply shows a happy sun icon every day, holding up a shiny gold trophy for being right almost every time. But just behind the robot, a single tiny rain cloud sneaks past completely unnoticed, with one small raindrop, the one event that actually mattered. The robot looks smug and oblivious. The style should be friendly and approachable, like an XKCD-inspired infographic crossed with a children's science book, expressive characters, minimal visual clutter. Suitable for a technical textbook. No text or lettering in the image. The humor should be gentle and immediately understandable. Keep the composition simple and focused on one clear visual metaphor: always predicting the common case scores high accuracy but misses the rare case that counts.
specs.alt: A smug desert weather forecaster robot holds a trophy for always predicting sun and being right nearly every day, while a single tiny rain cloud sneaks by unnoticed behind it, illustrating the accuracy paradox where a majority-only predictor scores high accuracy yet misses the rare class that actually matters.
specs.caption: Being right about the boring majority case is not the same as being useful; under imbalance, accuracy lets a useless model look excellent.

specs.anchorText: A startling fraction of training bugs are invisible in code and obvious in a picture
specs.prompt: Simple, cartoon-like educational illustration with clean lines and a warm color palette on a clean white background with generous margins: a diligent, hardworking cartoon robot student sits at a desk earnestly matching picture flashcards to name tags, but every name tag is shifted one slot to the right, so the robot is confidently pinning the dog's name on the cat's picture and the cat's name on the bird's picture. The robot looks proud and focused, completely unaware anything is wrong, with a little gold star sticker for effort. A small, slightly off-by-one row of cards makes the shift visually clear. The style should be friendly and approachable, like an XKCD-inspired infographic crossed with a children's science book, expressive characters, minimal visual clutter. Suitable for a technical textbook. No text or lettering in the image. The humor should be gentle and immediately understandable. Keep the composition simple and focused on one clear visual metaphor: a model diligently learning, but every label shifted by one.
specs.alt: A diligent cartoon robot student proudly matches picture cards to name tags, but every tag is shifted one slot over so it confidently labels the cat with the dog's name, illustrating the off-by-one label bug where a model trains perfectly while learning the wrong answer, the kind of pipeline bug a quick look at the data reveals.
specs.caption: A smoothly falling loss can mean the model is perfectly learning the wrong task; look at one real batch before you blame the optimizer.
